summary: At just 1.8 square miles, La Palma is one of the tiniest incorporated cities in Orange County — smaller than many golf courses — yet it packs in over 15,000 residents at a density north of 8,400 per square mile, giving it a compressed, walkable texture unusual for suburban southern California. The terrain is dead flat, a patch of the broad coastal plain between Buena Park and Cypress, and Central Park (the city's main green space) anchors the middle of town with ball fields and a community center reachable on foot from most directions. That compactness means errands stay short, but it also means La Palma is definitively a bedroom community: there is no major employment corridor within city limits, and commuters feed onto the 5 and 91 freeways — both notoriously congested — to reach job centers in Irvine, Anaheim, or downtown Los Angeles. The median home value of roughly $917,000 against a median household income near $116,000 yields a price-to-income ratio just under 8:1, meaning ownership demands either substantial savings or dual high-earning households, while median rent at $2,239 consumes about 23% of that same income, a relatively manageable ratio. Year-round highs averaging 76°F with nearly 9.5 hours of daily sunshine make the climate almost monotonously pleasant, and a violent crime rate of about 105 per 100,000 sits well below national averages. La Palma delivers the paradox of a place so small it barely registers on a map yet so expensive it demands serious financial gravity just to stay put.
